feedback: If a learner invokes an outward (centrifugal) force balancing gravity, redirect: gravity is the only force here; it bends the straight-line sideways motion into a curve, and that curve is the orbit.

Too slow: gravity curves the path down into the ground, so it falls back and crashes. Faster than circular speed but below escape speed: the path still closes, but stretches into an ellipse. At or above escape speed: gravity can't curve it enough to close the loop. Just right for a circle: the curve exactly follows the planet's surface shape.
Note that gravity sets how the path accelerates (curves), not the direction the ball is currently travelling — the ball keeps moving sideways while gravity pulls it inward.
activities.intendedInsight: An orbit results from sideways momentum plus a single inward gravitational pull that continually curves the path; there is no real outward force balancing gravity.
learnerActions: For a chosen launch, sketch or identify two arrows at the projectile: a forward (sideways) velocity arrow and an inward arrow pointing at the planet's centre for gravity.
Predict, before firing, whether a given speed will crash, circle, stretch into an ellipse or escape, and justify using the two arrows.

Explain why 'too slow' falls back and crashes, why a bit faster than circular speed stretches the orbit into an ellipse, why 'much too fast' (at or above escape speed) flies away, and what 'just right' for a circle means.
State explicitly that gravity is the only force acting on the ball in flight (in this idealised model) — there is no outward force holding it out.
activities.title: The momentum-vs-gravity tug-of-war

feedback: If a learner expects 'more speed just needs proportionally more fuel', have them compare two Δv settings and read off how disproportionately the fuel grows.
Reinforce the loop: more fuel adds more mass, which needs yet more fuel to move — this compounding is why the growth is so steep.
activities.intendedInsight: Because a rocket carries its unburned fuel, the propellant needed rises steeply (exponentially) with the demanded speed change — the qualitative heart of the rocket equation.
learnerActions: Set a target speed change (Δv) and watch the required propellant amount build up.

Increase the target Δv in steps and observe that the propellant needed grows faster than in proportion — doubling the demand always takes more than double the fuel, and far more than double once the Δv is large.
Explain in your own words why this happens: the rocket must lift and accelerate the fuel it hasn't burned yet, so extra fuel also needs its own fuel to be carried.
Describe why this means getting to orbit is hard and why large rockets are mostly fuel by mass.
activities.title: Fuel to carry fuel: why rockets are mostly propellant
